intro: Add every real location or service area your business operates in — a staffed office, a depot, or simply a town you regularly serve. For each one, answer the four evidence questions honestly. Nothing defaults to yes: an unanswered question counts as 'no' evidence, because a page built on a hopeful guess is exactly how thin, near-identical location pages happen in the first place.

evidenceCriteria.label: Staffed presence or a sustained local service base
evidenceCriteria.question: Does this location have a lease, a listed employee, a locally answered phone, or a real, ongoing history of completed jobs there — not just a plan to expand?
evidenceCriteria.whyItMatters: This is the difference between a real location and a dispatch entry. A city that only appears because a technician can drive there is not a staffed presence.

evidenceCriteria.label: Independently distinguishable content
evidenceCriteria.question: Is there something true of this location that is not equally true of every other one — a named local team, location-specific reviews, real local case examples, distinct hours or access notes?
evidenceCriteria.whyItMatters: A page whose only unique element is the city name in the heading is, by definition, the near-duplicate content Google's doorway-page policy targets.

evidenceCriteria.label: Genuinely separable search demand
evidenceCriteria.question: Would people search for this location plus your service in a way a single shared coverage page would not already answer?
evidenceCriteria.whyItMatters: If a combined 'services and coverage area' page already satisfies the query, a dedicated page competes with your own content rather than adding reach.

evidenceCriteria.label: A named owner who will keep it current
evidenceCriteria.question: Is there a specific person accountable for updating this page's local facts — staff, hours, reviews — as they change?
evidenceCriteria.whyItMatters: An unowned page decays into stale, near-identical content within a year, regardless of how well it was written on day one.

scoring.description: Each criterion scores yes=1, partial=0.5, no=0, summed across the four criteria per location (max score 4). The result is never shown as a percentage or grade — only used to sort the location into one of three classifications.

classifications.label: Flagship — build a dedicated page
classifications.message: This location clears the evidence test. It is a legitimate candidate for its own indexed page, provided the content-sufficiency checklist below is completed before publishing — not after.

classifications.label: Borderline — not yet, revisit later
classifications.message: This location has some real evidence but not enough yet. Publishing a page today would likely be thin; fold it into your coverage page for now and revisit once staffing, content or reviews genuinely change.

classifications.label: Coverage only — no dedicated page
classifications.message: This location does not yet clear the evidence test. List it as a named service area on your Google Business Profile and in your coverage page's town list instead of building a page for it.

sufficiencyChecklist.description: Before publishing any location marked 'flagship', confirm every item below is true for that specific page. A page missing more than one or two of these is not ready, regardless of its evidence score.

items.label: Opening paragraph is written specifically for this location and is not a copy of another location's page with the city name changed.
A phone number or contact route that reaches this specific location, not a generic head-office line.
At least one named local team member or a real photo of this location's team or premises.
Reviews or testimonials that explicitly reference this location or its team, not generic company-wide quotes reused across every page.
Opening hours, parking or access notes that are actually accurate for this address — not copied from the head office.
Address and phone number match this location's own Google Business Profile listing exactly.
A named person inside the business is responsible for reviewing and updating this page at least twice a year.
This page's title and heading target only this location, not the same phrase already targeted by the coverage page or another location page.

serviceAreaGuidance.description: For every location classified 'borderline' or 'coverage-only', use Google's own service-area business (SAB) mechanism instead of a dedicated page.
rules: If the business never serves walk-in customers at its address, remove the street address from the Google Business Profile entirely rather than display an address nobody is meant to visit.
Declare service areas as up to 20 named cities, postal codes or comparable areas — Google does not allow a plain radius setting.
Keep the outer boundary of declared areas within roughly two hours' driving time of the business's real base; areas further than that are a coverage-page mention at most, not a claimed service area.
Combine the profile with a single coverage page listing every served town on a map, rather than one page per town.

outputSummary.description: After all locations are scored, show three counts (flagship / borderline / coverage-only) and one plain-language recommendation for the overall site structure, never a single blended 'local SEO score.'

recommendationRules.message: None of your locations currently justify a dedicated page. Build one honest coverage page plus a correctly configured service-area profile, and stop there for now.
Build a dedicated page for each flagship location only. Everything else belongs on your coverage page and in your service-area profile, not as pages of its own.

You have enough genuine flagship locations to justify a systematic location-page template — but audit each one against the sufficiency checklist individually before publishing at this scale, since templates are exactly where near-duplicate content creeps back in.

disclaimer: This tool sorts the locations you enter using only the answers you provide. It does not scan your website, your Google Business Profile, or any search ranking data automatically, and it does not guarantee a ranking, indexing or traffic outcome. It is a structured starting point for a page-count decision, not an SEO audit, a legal opinion on Google's policies, or a guarantee against manual action. All processing happens locally in your browser; nothing you enter is transmitted or stored.
